newsitem.title: USA: Johnson & Johnson to buy Innotech.
newsitem.headline: Johnson & Johnson to buy Innotech.

text.p: Johnson & Johnson, in a move to grow its vision-care business, said Tuesday it had signed a definitive agreement to buy lens casting system maker Innotech Inc for $13.75 cash per share.
Roanoke, VA.-based Innotech's casting systems enable optical retailers to customize multifocal and single-vision prescription eyeglasses.

J&J said it will start a cash tender offer for Innotech's roughly nine million common shares within five days, and then acquire any remaining shares at the same price of $13.75 each in a second-step merger.
The boards of both companies have approved the deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, J&J said.

It also said a shareholder group holding about 3.3 million Innotech shares had agreed to tender its stock. The group consists of Chase Venture Capital Associates LP, CIBC Wood Gundy Ventures Inc, and Dr. Ronald Blum.
Innotech's options and warrants to buy about 850,000 shares will be cashed out in connection with offer, J&J said.
Innotech will pay J&J a $6.75 million break-up fee should the deal not be completed.
Innotech shares soared on news of the deal, rising to 13-3/4 from their Monday close at 8-7/8.
J&J shares were up 1/4 at 59-7/8.
J&J already owns about 5.0 percent of Innotech's shares, according to the two companies.
Innotech had revenues of $7.4 million for the first nine months of 1996, Steven Bennington, company president, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

He said the company had received no other acquisition offers but would consider other bids. "I think the process is that if somebody shows up that has something that's serious, we'd listen," Bennington said.
Innotech's flagship product -- the Excalibur SurfCasting System -- crafts high-end eyeglass lenses like biofocals and trifocals.

This business -- with a worldwide market of about $3 billion, according to industry observers -- is a departure for J&J, which derives most of its roughly $750 million in annual vision-care revenue from contact lenses, analysts said.

"They're going off on a different track here," said Robert Dunn, an analyst at Wasserstein Perella Securities. "It's not going to affect their earnings near-term, but it expands the scope of their eye-care business."
Dunn added, "They may have bought it at a good time, too, and they have the clout to take this thing worldwide really quickly."
Jeff Leebaw, a J&J spokesman, said the acquisition gives the company the chance to offer customers a choice between contact lenses and high-end eyeglasses.
Analysts said the acquisition was not necessarily a sign that J&J might move into other areas of vision care, such as surgery.
Leebaw declined comment, saying only, "I would not read any signals into this."
(( -- Jeff Mamera, New York Newsdesk 859-1700))
